passage: An analyst studying one professional basketball league argues that its offenses were remade during the 2010s. In the analyst's account, teams did not merely shoot more three-pointers as the decade went on; the shift toward the three-point line was accompanied by a league-wide rise in scoring efficiency. The analyst supports the claim with league averages from three seasons.

questionTable.caption: League-wide averages in one professional basketball league, selected seasons

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the claim?

choices.text: Teams attempted 34.1 three-pointers per game in the 2019-20 season, nearly double the 18.4 per game they had attempted in 2011-12.
Three-point attempts rose from 18.4 per game in 2011-12 to 24.1 in 2015-16 and 34.1 in 2019-20, while points per 100 possessions climbed from 104.6 to 106.4 to 110.6 over the same seasons.
Points per 100 possessions rose from 104.6 in 2011-12 to 106.4 in 2015-16 and 110.6 in 2019-20.
In the 2015-16 season, teams attempted 24.1 three-pointers per game and scored 106.4 points per 100 possessions, both higher than in 2011-12.

explanation:
**Choice B is correct.** The claim has two coupled parts — attempts shifted toward the three-point line, and efficiency rose alongside — and B is the only choice that traces both series across all three seasons.

**The Full Solution:**
- Part one of the claim: more three-pointers over the decade. B shows 18.4 to 24.1 to 34.1.
- Part two: scoring efficiency rose as the shift happened. B shows 104.6 to 106.4 to 110.6 over the same seasons.
- Presenting the two rises together is what makes the data support an "accompanied by" claim.

**Why the other choices are wrong:**
- A: It documents only the rise in attempts and says nothing about efficiency.
- C: It documents only the rise in efficiency and says nothing about attempts.
- D: A single season's pair of values, even with a comparison to 2011-12, cannot show two sustained trends moving together.
